## Logistic regression

At the core, ecology deals with complex systems: ecosystems are dynamic, interconnected, and often unpredictable. Research helps policymakers understand those complexities rather than relying on assumptions or short-term political pressures. Incorporating research into policy isn’t just a nice ideal in ecology—it’s often the difference between policies that work in the real world and ones that quietly fail or even make things worse. There are several reasons for having policy informed by literature including:

- Avoiding unintended consequences: Well-intentioned policies can backfire if they’re not grounded in evidence. Introducing a species to control pests, restricting fire use, or altering water flows have all caused ecological harm when research wasn’t adequately considered. Research helps anticipate trade-offs and second-order effects.
- Efficient use of limited resources: Conservation budgets are finite. Research helps identify what actually works—whether that’s habitat restoration methods, protected area placement, or invasive species control—so money and effort aren’t wasted on ineffective strategies.
- Credibility and public trust: Policies grounded in transparent, peer-reviewed research tend to be more defensible.

We are interested in drivers of whether a **review paper will be cited in policy or not**. We included all journals 2024 Web of Science  2024 JCR Biodiversity Conservation category journals, and included only review articles published in 2016-2020.

The dependent variable is if the review paper has been cited in policy as per the Overton database.
The potential predictors are: 

- Author count
- Number of citations
- Number of of pages
- Is the review available via Open Access
- Are any of the authors in government.


### Data processing {.unnumbered}

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
library(pROC) ## ROC curve
library(GGally)

## read in the data
papers_all <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop/refs/heads/main/data/review_paper_cited.csv", stringsAsFactors = T)


# Quick summaries
papers_all %>% summary()
## cited_in_policy is not 0/1 so we will need to convert it
## Some additional columns are here
## Some missing values, only 10 of 1148, we will drop them
## Several variables have extremes, do further quick checks on 
##  - author count
##  - times cited
##  - number of pages

# Histograms 
papers_all %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = author_count)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)

papers_all %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = times_cited)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)

papers_all %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_of_pages)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)
## take logs (in theory you can proceed with modelling without the transform and if you 
##  do you will see some issues.)

## Now make a  numeric version of cited (essential for modelling)
papers_all <- papers_all %>%
  mutate(
    cited_in_policy.n = if_else(cited_in_policy == "Y", 1, 0)
  )

# Check conversion
papers_all %>%
  count(cited_in_policy, cited_in_policy.n)

# Log transforms
papers_all <- papers_all %>%
  mutate(
    author_count.log = log(author_count),
    times_cited.log = log(times_cited + 1),
    n_of_pages.log   = log(n_of_pages)
  )

# Subset data (drop missing anygov + select columns)
papers <- papers_all %>%
  filter(!is.na(anygov)) %>%
  select(
    cited_in_policy.n,
    author_count.log,
    times_cited.log,
    n_of_pages.log,
    simple_OA,
    anygov
  )

## take a look
summary(papers_all)


```


Check the dimensions before proceeding, how many rows and columns do you expect the data to have?

### Modelling, Model Selection and Assumptions {.unnumbered}

In this section we will fit a logistic regression model, apply model selection if suitable, and check the assumptions and model diagnostics. 

There are some assumptions we should check before we do any modelling, these are detailed below.

```{r}

## take a quick look at the bivariate relationships before modelling
ggpairs(
  papers,
  lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", alpha = 0.6, size = 1)),
  upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 4)),
  diag  = list(continuous = wrap("densityDiag"))
) +
  theme_minimal()

```

| Assumption | Check         | Met       |                              
|:----------:|:-----------------------------------------:|:------------------:|
| Suitable outcome    | The outcome variable is either "successes" and "failures" (coded as 1 and 0 respectively), or counts of success and failures | This assumption is met.  ||
| Suitable amount of success and failures    | Here the numbers of reviews cited in policy and not cited are both large | This assumption is met.  |
| Multicolinearity    | In the scatterplots  we do not see any strong linear relationships between the numeric explanatory variables. | This assumption is  met.        |
| No complete separation   | This occurs when a predictor perfectly predicts the outcome, the pairs plots shows this is not the case for these papers | This assumption is met.  |
| Independence      | This data is published review papers. While some authors might contribute to more than one review article we in general don't expect that selection for citation in policy of one review influences the choice to select another review | This assumption is met.                  |

The initial checks suggest we can use logistic regression for this analysis so we proceed to run this and check further assumptions later on.



The null model is the intercept only model, and here we will test if the full model is better than this intercept only model. We will also look at the full model to see if model selection is worth exploring (if some explanatory variables are not statistically significant in the full model).



```{r}

## fit the full model
papers.glm <- glm(cited_in_policy.n ~ author_count.log + times_cited.log + n_of_pages.log + simple_OA + anygov, 
                  family = binomial,
                  data = papers)


## fit the null model
papers.glm.null <- glm(cited_in_policy.n ~1, 
                  family = binomial,
                  data = papers)

## Deviance goodness-of-fit test to test if this model is better than 
##  the null (intercept only model)
anova(papers.glm, papers.glm.null)
## this is a small p-value, therefore we note that the full model is better than an intercept only model

## summary of the model to see if we should apply model selection
summary(papers.glm)
## there are some terms which are not significant, explore model selection

## use the stepwise model selection approach
papers.glm.fin <- step(papers.glm.null, scope = (list(lower = papers.glm.null, upper = papers.glm)), 
                                            direction = "both", trace = T)

```

Now that we have a proposed final model we need to check some further assumptions.

Let's create the additional visualisations to allow us to evaluate the assumptions.

The figures below are as follows:

- The **fitted values versus the Pearsons residuals**. In this we are looking for an indication that there is change in the standardised residuals over the range of the fitted values to support an assessment of the assumption of equal variances. There should be an equal number of residual above zero and below zero, and not too many standardised residuals more extreme than -2 and 2. 

- **Leverage**: The plot of leverage versus the standardised residuals allows us to check if there are any large leverage points (leverage is how far a data point’s predictor values are from the “center” of all predictors) which also have large residuals. If there are any points with a large leverage and large residuals, these points are having an impact on the model and should be investigated further.


Overdispersion means there is more variability in the data than the model expects


```{r}

## look at the other diagnostics on the final model only

## check there is no problems with overdispersion
overdispersion <- sum(residuals(papers.glm, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(papers.glm)
overdispersion


## Fitted values
fittedv <- predict(papers.glm.fin, type = "response")

# Pearson residuals 
pearson_res <- residuals(papers.glm.fin, type = "pearson")

# Cook's distance
cooks_d <- cooks.distance(papers.glm.fin)

# Leverage (hat values)
lev <- hatvalues(papers.glm.fin)

# Standardised residuals (recommended)
std_res <- rstandard(papers.glm.fin)


# Create a data frame
diag_df <- data.frame(
  fittedv = fittedv,
  pearson_res = pearson_res,
  cooks_d = cooks_d,
  lev = lev,
  std_res = std_res
)

## Fitted values versus Pearsons residuals 
ggplot(diag_df, 
       aes(x = fittedv, y = pearson_res)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Review papers: fitted values vs pearsons residuals",
       x = "Fitted values",
       y = "Pearson residuals")


## Leverage and Cooks distance
n <- nrow(papers.glm.fin$model)

ggplot(diag_df, 
       aes(x = lev, y = std_res , colour = cooks_d> 4/n)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "red")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Review papers: leverage vs standardised residuals",
       x = "Leverage",
       y = "Standardised residuals",
       colour = "Influential")

max(abs(diag_df$cooks_d))
```




| Assumption | Check         | Met       |                              
|:----------:|:-----------------------------------------:|:------------------:|
| Overdispersion  | If overdispersion is more than 2 we need to account for this in the modelling, it is close to one.  |This assumption is met. |
| Pearson residuals checks   | We expect not too many Pearson residuals beyond -2 and 2.  |This assumption is met. |
| Influential points   | In the plot of leverage versus the standardised residuals three points might be of concern, but all are under 0.5 in terms of Cooks distance these are ok. |This assumption is met.|


All the assumptions are met. We can now look to see of the model is good at prediction.

```{r}

## Calculate the predicted and for now use 0.5 as the threshold for "success"
papers$prob_hat <- predict(papers.glm.fin, type = "response")
papers$pred <- ifelse(papers$prob_hat >0.5, 1, 0)

## present the confusion matrix
table(papers$pred, papers$cited_in_policy.n)

## present the ROC curve with AUC
roc_obj <- roc(papers$cited_in_policy.n, fitted(papers.glm.fin))
plot(roc_obj)
auc(roc_obj)

```

The true positive rate is 506/(179+506) = 0.74 and the false positive rate is 127/(326+127) =0.28. The area under the curve is 0.79. Therefore the model is good a predicting if a review article is cited in policy.


Now we look at the associations.

```{r}
summary(papers.glm.fin)

exp( 1.09554)
exp( 0.32737)
1-exp(-0.51676)

```


### Interpretation {.unnumbered}

For a one unit increase in the number of citations (on the log scale) we see a **300% increase in the odds of the review paper being cited in policy** (p-value <0.001). For a one unit increase in the count of authors (on the log scale) we see a 139% increase in the odds of the review paper being cited in policy (p-value <0.001). For a one unit increase in the number of pages (on the log scale) we see a 41% decrease in the odds of being cited in policy (p-value 0.001). 

The true positive rate is 74% and the false positive rate is 28%. The area under the curve is 0.79. Therefore the model is good a predicting if a review article is cited in policy.


## Beta regression

### Introduction {.unnumbered}

The journal level analyses used a **generalised linear model** with a **beta-binomial responses** with the outcome variables being the number of papers with policy citations and the number of papers without policy citations for each journal. The potential explanatory variable was the mean jounral impact factor (JIF). If model diagnostics suggested non-linear relationships a quadratic term was included for each of the explanatory variables. 

```{r}

library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
library(car)
library(ggeffects)
# web of science
# 
# All journals in the 2024  2024 JCR Biodiversity Conservation category.
# Year range is 2016-2020 (recent enough to be relevant, old enough for citations to accrue)
# Dependent variable is % of published papers per journal cited in policy as per the Overton database.
# Predictors: mean JIF

## DATA ANALYSIS SECTION
# Journal analysis
# JCR (sometimes WoSJournal)

# All journals in the 2024 JCR Biodiversity Conservation category.
# Year range is 2016-2020 (recent enough to be relevant, old enough for citations to accrue)
# Dependent variable is % of published papers per journal cited in policy as per the Overton database.
# Predictors: mean JIF, % papers OA

WoSJournal <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop/refs/heads/main/data/WoS_journal.csv")

WoSJournal <- WoSJournal[complete.cases(WoSJournal$N.papers.policy.cites),] ## was 57, now 56 obs

```


### Modelling and checks {.unnumbered}

After the data has been read into R, we do the modelling setup and run the model itself. For the beta regression, the most common option is to provide a count of the "successes" (here citations in policy) and "failures" (here no citation in policy). We are focussing on the primary research question and considering just mean JIF to see if there is a relationship between impact and policy citations. 


```{r}

## make a variable with how many journals have no citations
WoSJournal$N.papers.no.policy.cites <- WoSJournal$N.papers - WoSJournal$N.papers.policy.cites

## run the beta regression
WoSJournal_Journal_glm_bb1 <-  glmmTMB(cbind(N.papers.policy.cites, N.papers.no.policy.cites) ~Mean.JIF ,
                                 family = betabinomial(),
                                 data = WoSJournal)

```


Here we do some checked based on residuals simulated for the model. NOte that simulateResiduals creates scaled residuals by simulating from the fitted model and we can use those in model checking.


```{r}
## now do checks
sim_res_wos_bb1 <- simulateResiduals(WoSJournal_Journal_glm_bb1, n = 1000)
plot(sim_res_wos_bb1) ## small problem with upper quartile, check zero inflation, nonlinearity
```

There is clearly a problem, and it seems like there is a curve in the residuals. There are two possibilities we explore in terms of the causes of this:

- Zero-inflation: If there are too many publications with no citation that will cause a problem (less likely here)
- Non-linearity: The relationship is not linear but instead quadratic (the residuals shape is quadratic hence starting with this specific type of non-linearity).


```{r}

## zero inflation?
testZeroInflation(sim_res_wos_bb1) ## 0.096, probably not the problem as we suspected

## non-linearity, add a quadratic term: I(Mean.JIF^2)
WoSJournal_Journal_bb_nl <- glmmTMB(cbind(N.papers.policy.cites, N.papers.no.policy.cites) ~Mean.JIF +I(Mean.JIF^2),
                               family = betabinomial(),
                               data = WoSJournal,
                               control=glmmTMBControl(optCtrl=list(iter.max=1000))
)

## look again to see if it's helped
sim_res_wos_bb_nl <- simulateResiduals(WoSJournal_Journal_bb_nl, n = 1000)
plot(sim_res_wos_bb_nl) 
## does help this, one set is a little high but with one variable we can't do better 
```

### Visualisation {.unnumbered}

```{r}
## look at the model
summary(WoSJournal_Journal_bb_nl) 
## both terms significant

## visualise the model
pred_WoSJournal_Journal_glm_bb_JIF <- ggpredict(WoSJournal_Journal_bb_nl, terms = "Mean.JIF [all]")

ggplot(pred_WoSJournal_Journal_glm_bb_JIF, aes(x = x, y = predicted)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_point(
    data = WoSJournal,
    aes(
      x = Mean.JIF,
      y = N.papers.policy.cites / (N.papers.policy.cites + N.papers.no.policy.cites)
    ),
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  labs(
    y = "Probability of policy citation",
    x = "Mean JIF",
    title = "Relationship between JIF and policy citation"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal()


```

### Interpretation {.unnumbered}

We have significant evidence of a quadratic relationship between mean journal impact factor and the proportion of publications cited in policy (p-value 0.014). The visualisation shows that as journal impact factor increases so too does the probability of a policy citation, however this effect does not continue for high impact factors (those over 5).


:::


# Assessment {.unnumbered}

Task to complete before the end of the workshop.

We are interested in predicting  if a newly detected terrestrial species is native (1) or not (0) to a ecologically fragile environment. We have information on these species including:

- Diet: 1 is the species is a generalist, 0 is specialist
- Diurnal: 1 is mainly diurnal, 0 is mainly nocturnal
- Colonial: 1 is colonial, 0 is solitary
- Agriculture: 1 the species is known and controlled in commercial agriculture, 0 it is not
- Flight: 1 the species can fly, 0 the species can not fly

First download the `native_alien.csv` file on [GitHub](https://github.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop) in the ‘data’ folder and load it in R.


Your tasks are to:

**1. Fit a suitable model and create the  visualisations for diagnostics checking**


**2. Assess if each assumption is met for the final model**


**3. Provide a summary of the model and detail if the model is suitable for prediction**


```{r ans 1 hide, include=FALSE}
## read in the data

native <- read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop/refs/heads/main/data/native_alien.csv')


## take a look
summary(native)

## simple data, look at some tables
table(native$status)
table(native$status, native$Diet)
table(native$status, native$Diurnal)
table(native$status, native$Colonial)
table(native$status, native$Agriculture)
table(native$status, native$Flight)

## Assumptions

## Suitable outcome: Yes, native or alien 
## Suitable amount of success and failures: Yes, 91 natives and 583 aliens
## Multicolinearity: Not relevant
## No complete separation: None seen
## Independence: Assume each species arrives at the location independently

## fit the full model
native.glm <- glm(status ~ Diet + Diurnal + Colonial + Agriculture + Flight, 
                  family = binomial,
                  data = native)


## fit the null model
native.glm.null <- glm(status ~1, 
                  family = binomial,
                  data = native)

## Deviance goodness-of-fit test to test if this model is better than 
##  the null (intercept only model)
anova(native.glm, native.glm.null)
## this is a small p-value, therefore we note that the full model is better than an intercept only model

## summary of the model to see if we should apply model selection
summary(native.glm)
## there are some terms which are not significant, explore model selection

## use the stepwise model selection approach
native.glm.fin <- step(native.glm.null, scope=(list(lower =native.glm.null, upper = native.glm)), 
                                            direction = "both", trace = T)


## look at the other diagnostics on the final model only

## check there is no problems with overdispersion
overdispersion <- sum(residuals(native.glm.fin, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(native.glm.fin)
overdispersion


## Fitted values
fittedv.native <- predict(native.glm.fin, type = "response")

# Pearson residuals 
pearson_res.native <- residuals(native.glm.fin, type = "pearson")

# Cook's distance
cooks_d.native <- cooks.distance(native.glm.fin)

# Leverage (hat values)
lev.native <- hatvalues(native.glm.fin)

# Standardised residuals (recommended)
std_res.native <- rstandard(native.glm.fin)


# Create a data frame
diag_df_native <- data.frame(
  fittedv = fittedv.native,
  pearson_res = pearson_res.native,
  cooks_d = cooks_d.native,
  lev = lev.native,
  std_res = std_res.native
)

## Fitted values versus Pearsons residuals 
ggplot(diag_df_native, 
       aes(x = fittedv, y = pearson_res)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Native species: fitted values vs pearsons residuals",
       x = "Fitted values",
       y = "Pearson residuals")


## Leverage and Cooks distance
n.native <- nrow(native.glm.fin$model)

ggplot(diag_df_native, 
       aes(x = lev, y = std_res , colour = cooks_d> 4/n.native)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "red")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Native species: leverage vs standardised residuals",
       x = "Leverage",
       y = "Standardised residuals",
       colour = "Influential")

max(abs(diag_df_native$cooks_d))


## Assumption

## Overdispersion  0.73 so no concerns
## Pearson residuals checks: Some high values
## Leverage: Also some high values

## Likely the result of so many categorical variable, if stable continue


## Calculate the predicted and for now use 0.5 as the threshold for "success"
native$prob_hat <- predict(native.glm.fin, type = "response")
native$pred <- ifelse(native$prob_hat >0.5, 1, 0)

## present the confusion matrix
table(native$pred, native$status)

## present the ROC curve with AUC
roc_obj_native <- roc(native$status, fitted(native.glm.fin))
plot(roc_obj_native)
auc(roc_obj_native)

# Area under the curve: 0.8951

summary(native.glm.fin)

1-exp( -3.0050)
exp( 1.9735)
exp(1.4721 )
1-exp( -0.4497 )
```
